narrationPlan.voice: One clear, warm narrator throughout; no character voices
narrationPlan.pace: Stately, clear, and proud (about 125 words per minute)
notes: Read as a single narrator: this is a science article, not a story with characters.
Pause for two seconds at each comprehension check so learners can reason first.
Say numbers and units in full ("one hundred and fifty million kilometres", "astronomical units") and pronounce names clearly.

Original article written for Ghanaian JHS learners from widely known history and oral tradition. It is not copied from any book.

Local accuracy: the Golden Stool (Sika Dwa Kofi) is sacred; no one sits on it. Akwasidae falls every sixth Sunday. Manhyia Palace in Kumasi is the seat of the Asantehene. Teach the descent of the stool as tradition.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated JHS age band (Basic 7 to Basic 9) and BECE conceptual level?
Are all facts, figures, and dates accurate and up to date at the time of publication?
Ask a historian or the Manhyia Palace Museum to confirm dates and names.
Check that the Golden Stool is described with respect and that no picture shows anyone sitting on it.

teacherGuide.overview: Tells how Asante was united around the Golden Stool, how it governed and traded, and how it resisted British rule.
learningGoals: Name the founders of the Asante kingdom and explain the role of the Golden Stool.
Describe how Asante was governed and what it traded.
Outline the conflict with Britain from 1824 to 1900.
Explain what a shared symbol does for a nation.

beforeReading: Ask: what objects or symbols make you feel that you belong to Ghana? List them.
whileReading: After Page 3, discuss: why was a story more powerful than an order from Osei Tutu would have been?
afterReading: Learners draw a timeline from 1701 to 1935 and mark five events.
discussion: Yaa Asantewaa spoke when the chiefs were silent. What made her able to do so?
reflection: Is there something you would defend even if others around you hesitated?

mathsExtension.task: Prempeh I was sent away in 1896 and returned in 1924. How many years was he in exile?
Akwasidae comes every 42 days. About how many times does it fall in a year of 365 days?

support: Give learners five picture cards (stool, battle, burning town, queen mother, returning king) to order as they listen.
stretch: Find out the meanings of three adinkra symbols and when each is used.

factCheck.claim: Battle of Feyiase (c. 1701), Anglo-Asante wars (1824, 1874, 1900), exile of Prempeh I (1896–1924), and restoration of the Asante union (1935).
factCheck.explanation: Dates used (Feyiase about 1701; wars of 1824 and 1874; exile 1896; war of 1900; return 1924; restoration 1935) come from general historical knowledge and should be confirmed by a historian. The descent of the Golden Stool is oral tradition.
factCheck.reference: NaCCA CCP Social Studies curriculum (NaCCA, 2021) B9.3.3.1.1; Primary History B4.2.5.1.1.

pronunciation.guidance: roughly "mahn-HYEE-ah". The "nhy" consonant cluster has no exact English equivalent.
reviewerNotes: HIGH RISK: "nhy" cluster needs native-speaker demonstration.

pronunciation.guidance: a single long "YAAH" (the double a marks a long vowel).
reviewerNotes: Confirm vowel length; engines may shorten it to "ya".
Confirm stress and final long vowel.
